flashcards.front: Verifying a custom domain in Microsoft 365
flashcards.back: You add the custom domain in the admin center, then Microsoft 365 gives you a unique TXT record value to add at your DNS host. Once the TXT record is published and detected, the domain is verified and you can add MX, CNAME (Autodiscover), and SPF records to route mail and enable services.
flashcards.detail: Domain verification only proves ownership; it does not by itself move mail flow. You still have to update MX records at the DNS host to actually route mail through Exchange Online.

flashcards.front: Group-based licensing vs. direct (per-user) licensing
flashcards.back: Group-based licensing assigns a license to a Microsoft Entra security group, and every current and future member of that group automatically inherits it. Direct licensing assigns a license to one user at a time and must be repeated for each new hire or role change.
flashcards.detail: Group-based licensing scales far better for onboarding/offboarding at volume, since adding or removing a user from the group is the only step needed — no separate license action.

flashcards.front: Disabling an individual service plan within a license
flashcards.back: A license SKU (like Microsoft 365 E3) bundles many service plans (Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Viva Engage, Stream, etc.). An admin can disable specific service plans for a user or group while keeping the rest of the license active, instead of removing the whole license.
flashcards.detail: This is how you grant everything else in a bundle while withholding one workload a user should not have — for example, disabling the Viva Engage service plan (formerly Yammer) for a group that should not use it.

flashcards.front: Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP) vs. classic Delegated Admin Privileges (DAP)
flashcards.back: GDAP lets a Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) partner be granted only the specific, time-bound Microsoft Entra roles it needs to support a customer tenant, following least-privilege principles. Classic DAP granted the partner broad Admin Agent access (effectively Global Administrator) across the whole tenant with no expiration.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft deprecated DAP in favor of GDAP (partners could no longer manage DAP relationships from late 2023) specifically because DAP's all-or-nothing, non-expiring access violated least-privilege administration.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Apps update channels: Current, Monthly Enterprise, Semi-Annual Enterprise
flashcards.back: Current Channel delivers new features to users as soon as they are ready (roughly monthly, with feature updates arriving unpredictably). Monthly Enterprise Channel delivers the same features but bundled once a month on a predictable, fixed release date. Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel delivers feature updates only twice a year, for organizations that need the most validation time before rollout.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft recommends Monthly Enterprise Channel when you want features every month but need to know the release date in advance (the second Tuesday), and reserves Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel for select devices that need extensive testing before new features arrive.

flashcards.front: Shared mailbox vs. distribution group vs. Microsoft 365 group
flashcards.back: A shared mailbox is a single mailbox multiple people can send/receive from with delegated permissions (no license required if under the size limit). A distribution group only routes mail to its members' own inboxes. A Microsoft 365 group is a broader membership object that also provisions a shared mailbox, a SharePoint site, a Planner, and other connected resources.
flashcards.detail: A common exam trap is treating a distribution group as if it stores mail — it does not; mail sent to it simply fans out to each member's own mailbox.

flashcards.front: SharePoint Online external sharing levels
flashcards.back: SharePoint external sharing can be set (at the organization level, and then narrowed per site) to Anyone (anonymous links), New and existing guests (requires sign-in or verification), Existing guests only, or Only people in your organization. Each site's sharing level can never be more permissive than the org-wide setting.
flashcards.detail: This layered model means the org-wide setting acts as a ceiling: tightening it at the tenant level immediately restricts what any individual site admin can allow, regardless of that site's own configuration.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 network connectivity endpoint categories
flashcards.back: Microsoft 365 network endpoints are published as Optimize (highest volume/latency-sensitive, like Teams media and Exchange — should bypass proxies/VPNs), Allow (required but lower priority), and Default (general Microsoft 365 traffic that can be routed like normal internet traffic).
flashcards.detail: Routing Optimize category endpoints through a traditional on-premises proxy or VPN hairpin is the classic cause of poor Teams call quality, since it adds latency to traffic Microsoft explicitly says should take the most direct path.

flashcards.front: Security defaults vs. Conditional Access
flashcards.back: Security defaults are a free, one-size-fits-all baseline (requiring MFA registration for all users, blocking legacy authentication, and similar protections) that cannot be customized. Conditional Access is a licensed (Entra ID P1/P2) policy engine that lets you build granular if-then rules based on user, app, device, location, and risk.
flashcards.detail: Security defaults and Conditional Access are mutually exclusive per tenant — enabling Conditional Access policies requires turning security defaults off, since Conditional Access is meant to fully replace that baseline with tailored rules.

flashcards.front: Password hash sync vs. pass-through authentication vs. federation
flashcards.back: Password hash sync (PHS) synchronizes a hash of the on-premises password hash to Microsoft Entra ID so sign-in is validated in the cloud. Pass-through authentication (PTA) validates the password directly against on-premises Active Directory via lightweight agents, with no password hash stored in the cloud. Federation (e.g., AD FS) delegates authentication entirely to an external identity provider.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft recommends password hash sync (often paired with seamless SSO) as the default hybrid identity method for most organizations, since it is the simplest to operate and, because the hashes reach Entra ID, it also enables leaked-credential detection in Entra ID Protection and works as a fallback if on-premises authentication is unavailable.

flashcards.front: Conditional Access grant controls vs. session controls
flashcards.back: Grant controls decide whether access is allowed at all, and under what conditions (require MFA, require a compliant device, require a hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device, block access). Session controls apply restrictions during an already-granted session (like Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps app enforced restrictions or limiting sign-in frequency).
flashcards.detail: A policy can combine both: grant access only if MFA is satisfied (a grant control), then also restrict that session to browser-only, no-download access (a session control) for an unmanaged device.

flashcards.front: Defender for Office 365: Safe Links vs. Safe Attachments
flashcards.back: Safe Links rewrites URLs in email and Office documents so that each click is checked against threat intelligence at the time of click, not just at delivery time. Safe Attachments detonates attachments in an isolated sandbox environment before delivery to catch malware that static scanning would miss.
flashcards.detail: Safe Links' time-of-click protection is what defeats a delayed-activation phishing link — one that was clean when the email arrived but was weaponized by the attacker afterward.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender XDR unified incident correlation
flashcards.back: Microsoft Defender XDR correlates signals across Defender for Office 365, Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity, and Defender for Cloud Apps into a single unified incident in the Microsoft Defender portal, instead of leaving admins to manually connect related alerts from each product separately.
flashcards.detail: An exam scenario describing an attack that touches email, an endpoint, and identity sign-in behavior is pointing at the unified incident view in Defender XDR as the place to investigate the full attack chain in one place.

flashcards.front: Data loss prevention (DLP) policy anatomy
flashcards.back: A Microsoft Purview DLP policy defines locations (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams chat, endpoint devices), conditions that detect sensitive content (like matching a sensitive information type such as a credit card number), and actions/rules (block sharing, show a policy tip, restrict access, or require an override justification).
flashcards.detail: DLP policies can run in simulation mode first (with or without policy tips shown to users) before being enforced, which is the recommended way to tune false positives before the policy starts blocking real business activity.

flashcards.front: Retention policy vs. retention label
flashcards.back: A retention policy applies the same retain/delete rule broadly across a whole location (a mailbox, a SharePoint site, a Teams channel) without users needing to do anything. A retention label is applied to individual items (by a user or automatically via a trainable classifier or sensitive-info match) so different content in the same location can have different retention behavior.
flashcards.detail: When a policy and a label disagree about how long to keep an item, the longer retention period generally wins, and an explicit "retain" instruction generally wins over a "delete" instruction — content is preserved by default when rules conflict.

flashcards.front: Sensitivity label vs. retention label
flashcards.back: A sensitivity label classifies and protects content itself — it can apply encryption, add a watermark or header/footer, and restrict permissions, and it travels with the file. A retention label governs the lifecycle of the content — how long it must be kept or when it must be deleted — and does not by itself add any protection to the content.
flashcards.detail: The two are independent and can both be applied to the same document at once: a sensitivity label encrypting it as "Confidential" while a separate retention label governs when it can eventually be deleted.

flashcards.front: eDiscovery Standard vs. eDiscovery Premium
flashcards.back: eDiscovery (Standard) lets you create cases, search content across locations, and export results for basic legal hold and search scenarios. eDiscovery Premium (part of Microsoft Purview) adds custodian management, legal hold notifications, advanced review sets, analytics (near-duplicate detection, email threading, themes), and review workflow features for complex litigation.
flashcards.detail: A scenario describing custodian communications, hold notifications, or analytics like near-duplicate/threading is pointing specifically at Premium — Standard search-and-export alone cannot do custodian-level workflow.

flashcards.front: Insider Risk Management
flashcards.back: Insider Risk Management uses signals (like unusual file downloads, mass deletions, or data exfiltration to personal accounts) combined with HR data (such as resignation or termination events) to surface and score potentially risky internal user activity, without exposing individual reviewers to unnecessary personal detail via pseudonymization.
flashcards.detail: Pseudonymization of user identities in case alerts, until an investigator explicitly needs to reveal them, is a specific control meant to balance risk detection against employee privacy during the review process.

flashcards.front: Communication compliance
flashcards.back: Communication compliance scans internal and external communications (email, Teams chats, third-party connectors) for policy violations like harassment, sensitive data sharing, or regulatory language, routing flagged items to reviewers instead of blocking the message outright.
flashcards.detail: Unlike DLP, communication compliance is a detect-and-review workflow, not a real-time block — it is meant to surface conduct and compliance risk for human review, not to stop a message from sending.

flashcards.front: Audit (Standard) vs. Audit (Premium)
flashcards.back: Audit (Standard) retains audit records for 180 days by default and covers a broad set of crucial events across Microsoft 365 services. Audit (Premium) builds on it with audit log retention policies, retention of up to one year by default for E5-licensed users (up to ten years with an add-on), intelligent insights, and higher bandwidth access to the Office 365 Management Activity API.
flashcards.detail: An investigation asking exactly which items in a mailbox were read after a suspected compromise needs the "MailItemsAccessed" event. Microsoft rolled that event (along with Send) out to Audit (Standard) in 2024, so the deciding factor in scenarios is usually retention: Standard's 180 days versus Premium's one year.

flashcards.front: Information barriers
flashcards.back: Information barriers are Microsoft Purview policies that explicitly restrict which users or groups can communicate and collaborate with each other in Teams and OneDrive/SharePoint, used to prevent conflicts of interest (for example, keeping an investment banking team from chatting with a research team).
flashcards.detail: Information barriers actively block communication and content discovery between defined segments, which makes them a different kind of control from Conditional Access, which governs the conditions for signing in rather than who can talk to whom.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Secure Score
flashcards.back: Secure Score is a measurement of an organization's security posture, expressed as a numeric score, based on completed security actions (like enabling MFA or turning on a Conditional Access policy) weighed against recommended improvement actions across identity, devices, apps, and data.
flashcards.detail: Secure Score recommendations link directly to the admin console page needed to implement them, and the score updates automatically as configuration changes are detected, rather than needing a manual re-scan trigger.

flashcards.front: Compliance Manager and compliance score
flashcards.back: Compliance Manager translates regulatory and internal-policy requirements into actionable improvement actions, tracked as a compliance score, and distinguishes Microsoft-managed actions (already fulfilled by the service) from your-responsibility actions that your organization must implement and attest to.
flashcards.detail: The split between Microsoft-managed and customer-managed actions reflects the shared responsibility model — Microsoft attests to its own controls, but a customer-responsibility action (like configuring a DLP policy) still needs your organization to implement and document it.

flashcards.front: Role-based access control (RBAC) in Microsoft Purview
flashcards.back: Purview permissions can be granted through role groups (built-in, like Compliance Administrator, or custom) in addition to Microsoft Entra roles, letting you grant scoped access to specific compliance solutions (like eDiscovery or DLP) without granting broader Microsoft 365 admin rights.
flashcards.detail: A user can hold zero Microsoft Entra admin roles and still fully manage DLP policies, because Purview role groups are a separate permission layer purpose-built for compliance solutions.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Copilot licensing prerequisites
flashcards.back: Microsoft 365 Copilot (now called Microsoft Copilot in Microsoft documentation) requires an eligible base subscription (such as Microsoft 365 E3/E5, Business Standard/Premium, or A3/A5) plus the Copilot add-on license assigned to each user; Microsoft 365 E7 includes it. Simply owning the base subscription does not grant Copilot access on its own.
flashcards.detail: Because Copilot is an add-on rather than a standalone SKU, group-based licensing is the recommended way to roll it out to a pilot group or department cleanly, the same as any other add-on license.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Copilot and the Semantic Index
flashcards.back: The Semantic Index is a Microsoft Graph-based, encrypted index of an organization's content and relationships (files, emails, chats, meetings) that Copilot uses to understand context and ground its responses in organizational data, going beyond simple keyword search.
flashcards.detail: Because results from the Semantic Index are trimmed to content the requesting user already has permission to access, it is a grounding mechanism, not an access-granting one — it cannot surface content the user could not already open.

flashcards.front: Copilot respects existing permissions (no new access is granted)
flashcards.back: Microsoft 365 Copilot only surfaces organizational content in its responses that the requesting user already has at least view permission to, honoring the same permissions model as SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange. Copilot does not grant any new access a user did not already have.
flashcards.detail: This is exactly why pre-existing oversharing (files broadly shared with "Anyone" or "Everyone except external users" links) becomes a real risk with Copilot — it surfaces what already-overshared access allows, rather than creating a new vulnerability itself.

flashcards.front: Restricted SharePoint Search and oversharing remediation
flashcards.back: Restricted SharePoint Search limits organization-wide search and Copilot to an admin-curated allowed list of sites (up to 100), so sites left off the list drop out of those results without any change to user permissions. It was designed as a temporary mitigation while a broader oversharing review is completed. Microsoft has announced its retirement (new enablement blocked from July 31, 2026; fully retired January 31, 2027) and recommends Restricted Content Discovery, which hides individual sites instead.
flashcards.detail: This is a search-visibility control, not a permissions control — a user who already has direct access to a site that is not on the allowed list can still open it directly, and content the user owns, recently opened, or had shared directly may still be discoverable.

flashcards.front: Data Security Posture Management for AI (DSPM for AI)
flashcards.back: DSPM for AI, in Microsoft Purview (now the classic version, succeeded by the current Data Security Posture Management experience with AI observability), gives admins visibility into how users are interacting with AI apps (like Microsoft 365 Copilot and other generative AI tools), surfaces oversharing and sensitive-data risks, and recommends or auto-applies policies (DLP, sensitivity labels) tailored to AI usage.
flashcards.detail: DSPM for AI is specifically built to close the gap where an org already had DLP and labeling, but had no visibility into how those controls interact with prompts, grounding data, and generated responses in AI tools.

flashcards.front: DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot
flashcards.back: Purview DLP policies can use the Microsoft 365 Copilot location in two ways: a condition on sensitivity labels stops Copilot from processing labeled files and emails (so their content is not summarized or quoted), and a condition on sensitive information types stops Copilot from processing prompts that contain that data (including using them for web searches). The user's own file access is unaffected.
flashcards.detail: This lets an admin allow a user to keep normal file access while still preventing a labeled file's content specifically from being summarized or quoted back by Copilot — a narrower control than removing file access outright.

flashcards.front: Copilot Control System
flashcards.back: The Copilot Control System (documented as Copilot controls) is the umbrella set of admin capabilities (in the Microsoft 365 admin center, Power Platform admin center, Copilot Studio and Purview) for governing Copilot and AI agents across the tenant, in three pillars: Security and governance, Management controls, and Measurement and reporting.
flashcards.detail: It is a governance framework spanning multiple admin surfaces rather than a single console — an exam question describing where to manage Copilot readiness, agent oversight, and usage reporting together is describing this system conceptually, even though the actual settings live across the Microsoft 365 admin center and Purview portal.

flashcards.front: Copilot agents and Copilot Studio
flashcards.back: A Copilot agent is a focused, purpose-built extension of Copilot (answering questions from a specific knowledge source, or automating a specific task) that can be built with little to no code in Copilot Studio, or created directly from a SharePoint site or declarative agent template, then published for use in Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, or other surfaces.
flashcards.detail: Agents built directly from a SharePoint site are grounded only in that site's content and inherit its existing permissions, making them a lightweight option compared to a full custom agent built in Copilot Studio with its own connectors and topics.

flashcards.front: Agent identity in Microsoft Entra Agent ID
flashcards.back: Microsoft Entra Agent ID gives AI agents their own identity objects in Microsoft Entra ID (agent identities created from an agent identity blueprint, optionally with an agent's user account), so agents can be discovered, governed through sponsors, access packages and Conditional Access, and monitored like any other identity rather than being invisible to identity governance.
flashcards.detail: Giving agents first-class identities is what lets admins apply the same governance patterns to them as to human and application identities — access reviews, lifecycle policies, and Conditional Access-style oversight, rather than agents being an ungoverned blind spot.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Security Copilot and Security Compute Units (SCUs)
flashcards.back: Microsoft Security Copilot is a standalone generative AI assistant for security teams (distinct from Microsoft 365 Copilot) that integrates with Defender, Entra, Purview, and Intune to help summarize incidents, investigate threats, and generate scripts or reports. It is billed on a consumption basis using Security Compute Units (SCUs), which are provisioned capacity rather than a per-user license; Microsoft 365 E5 now also includes a monthly SCU allotment scaled to the number of E5 users.
flashcards.detail: Because Security Copilot uses SCU-based consumption pricing rather than per-user licensing, capacity can be provisioned and scaled up or down independently of how many named users are assigned to it.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Graph connectors for Copilot grounding
flashcards.back: Microsoft Graph connectors (now branded Microsoft 365 Copilot connectors) index content from external and third-party data sources (like a wiki, a ticketing system, or a file share outside Microsoft 365) into Microsoft Search and the Semantic Index, so Copilot can ground its answers in that external content too, subject to the same permission-trimming as native content.
flashcards.detail: A connector's permission mapping to the source system's own access control list is what preserves the "no new access" guarantee when grounding Copilot on non-Microsoft-365 content — a misconfigured connector that maps permissions incorrectly is a real oversharing risk.

flashcards.front: Insider risk management for AI interactions
flashcards.back: Insider Risk Management can include AI-specific indicators, such as risky or policy-violating prompts submitted to Copilot or other generative AI tools, as signals contributing to a user's overall risk score, alongside traditional indicators like file exfiltration.
flashcards.detail: This extends insider risk coverage beyond file and email activity into the prompts and interactions users have with AI tools themselves, since a risky intent can now show up in a prompt before any file is ever touched.

flashcards.front: Auditing and eDiscovery for Copilot interactions
flashcards.back: Microsoft 365 Copilot prompts and responses are captured as audit log events and can be searched, exported, and placed on legal hold through Microsoft Purview eDiscovery, just like other Microsoft 365 content, giving compliance teams visibility into what users asked Copilot and what it returned.
flashcards.detail: This audit trail is what makes Copilot interactions discoverable in litigation or an internal investigation — an interaction is treated as a compliance-relevant record, not an ephemeral, unlogged exchange.

flashcards.front: Responsible AI oversight of AI agents in the tenant
flashcards.back: Governing AI agents responsibly in a Microsoft 365 tenant means applying the same admin discipline used elsewhere: inventorying which agents exist, reviewing their data access and permissions, monitoring their usage and behavior, and being able to disable or remove an agent that behaves unexpectedly or accesses data it should not.
flashcards.detail: Treating agent oversight as an ongoing lifecycle process (discover, review, monitor, remediate) rather than a one-time approval at creation is the responsible-AI framing the exam expects, mirroring how app governance already treats third-party applications.

flashcards.front: Message trace
flashcards.back: An Exchange Online tool that follows a specific email through the mail flow pipeline, showing exactly when it was received, what rules or policies acted on it, and where it ended up — delivered, quarantined, or dropped.
flashcards.detail: This is the first stop for 'did my email actually send/arrive' tickets, before escalating further into Defender for Office 365's Threat Explorer for anything security-related.

flashcards.front: Content explorer
flashcards.back: A Microsoft Purview tool showing exactly which items across the tenant currently carry a given sensitivity label or match specific sensitive information types, letting an admin see the real scope of sensitive content before or after rolling out a policy.
flashcards.detail: This is where you'd confirm that the sensitive information types or labels a DLP policy relies on actually match the content you think they do, rather than assuming from the policy definition alone.

flashcards.front: Mail flow rules (transport rules)
flashcards.back: Exchange Online rules that inspect messages in transit and take an action — add a disclaimer, redirect, block, or apply encryption — based on conditions like sender, recipient, or message content.
flashcards.detail: A Message trace shows what actually happened to one message after the fact; a mail flow rule is what decides what happens to messages matching a condition going forward.

flashcards.front: Activity explorer
flashcards.back: A Microsoft Purview tool showing what actually happened to labeled or sensitive content over time — copied, printed, shared externally — as opposed to Content explorer’s snapshot of where that content currently sits.
flashcards.detail: Content explorer answers "where is this sensitive content right now"; Activity explorer answers "what has been done with it" — both draw on the same underlying classification.

flashcards.front: Litigation hold vs. retention policy
flashcards.back: A litigation hold is applied to an individual mailbox to preserve all its content indefinitely (or for a set period) for legal reasons, independent of any organization-wide policy. A retention policy or retention label, by contrast, applies a consistent retain/delete rule across a broader set of content.
flashcards.detail: A litigation hold on one mailbox can keep content longer than what an organization-wide retention policy would otherwise delete — the more restrictive (longer-retaining) rule always wins when both apply.

flashcards.front: Priority accounts
flashcards.back: Priority accounts are a Microsoft Defender for Office 365 feature: an admin tags specific users (executives, VIPs) with the Priority account tag, and Defender applies extra protection heuristics and shows the tag in reports, Threat Explorer, and campaign views so these frequently targeted mailboxes are easy to watch.
flashcards.detail: Flagging an account as priority doesn't grant it any extra license or permission — it only adds visibility and protection tuning in Defender for Office 365. Insider Risk Management has its own, separate priority user groups feature.

flashcards.front: Auto-labeling for sensitivity labels
flashcards.back: Service-side auto-labeling policies scan content in Exchange, SharePoint, and OneDrive for matching sensitive information types (like credit card numbers) and apply a sensitivity label automatically, instead of relying on everyone to label content by hand. (Recommending a label to the user is a separate, client-side auto-labeling option in Office apps.)
flashcards.detail: Policies are tested in simulation mode first, and applying a label across existing SharePoint and OneDrive content is not instant; confirming which files actually picked up a label is a job for Content explorer, not the auto-labeling policy's own configuration screen.

flashcards.front: Customer Lockbox
flashcards.back: Customer Lockbox requires a Microsoft support engineer to get explicit customer approval before accessing tenant content during a support request, rather than relying only on Microsoft's own internal access controls.
flashcards.detail: It only applies to a narrow set of support scenarios where a human engineer would need direct access to customer data — most support and service operations never need this, and Lockbox never triggers for them.

flashcards.front: Attack simulation training
flashcards.back: Attack simulation training in Defender for Office 365 lets an administrator launch realistic, safe phishing, credential-harvest, or malware-attachment campaigns against real users, then automatically enrolls anyone who falls for it into targeted training.
flashcards.detail: Simulation reports show which users clicked, reported, or ignored the message, so a user who repeatedly fails simulations is a real, measurable signal to target with training, not just a training-completion checkbox.

flashcards.front: Domain reuse during a tenant-to-tenant migration
flashcards.back: A custom domain can only be verified in one Microsoft 365 tenant at a time, so before it can be added and reverified in a destination tenant it must first be removed from the source tenant's verified domains. Until the domain's DNS records are cut over to the destination tenant, mail addressed to that domain continues routing to the source tenant.
flashcards.detail: Because removing the domain from the source tenant immediately stops it from accepting mail there, the domain cutover is normally planned as the last, tightly timed step of a migration — after mailbox content and permissions have already landed in the destination tenant.

flashcards.front: Least-privilege delegation with built-in Microsoft 365 admin roles
flashcards.back: Built-in roles like Helpdesk Administrator, User Administrator, License Administrator, and Exchange Administrator grant narrower, task-specific rights than Global Administrator, letting front-line staff perform routine actions (like resetting a non-admin user's password) without tenant-wide control. Custom Microsoft Entra roles can narrow permissions even further when no built-in role fits exactly.
flashcards.detail: Helpdesk Administrator cannot reset passwords for users who themselves hold admin roles — a scenario asking who can reset a Global Administrator's forgotten password is pointing at a higher-privilege role or the affected admin's own recovery options, not Helpdesk Administrator.

flashcards.front: Service health vs. Message center in the Microsoft 365 admin center
flashcards.back: Service health reports the real-time operational status of each Microsoft 365 service — active incidents, advisories, and resolution timelines — so admins can confirm whether a problem is a known Microsoft-side issue. Message center instead posts upcoming and recently rolled-out changes, new features, and deprecations that admins need to plan for, independent of whether anything is currently broken.
flashcards.detail: A user reporting that a familiar feature suddenly "looks different" or "stopped working" is often not an outage at all — checking Message center for a recently announced feature rollout explains many such tickets that Service health will show nothing for.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra Connect vs. Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync
flashcards.back: Microsoft Entra Connect is a full-featured, server-based sync engine that supports complex custom sync rules and can synchronize multiple connected forests, but it takes more hands-on management. Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync instead uses lightweight agents managed mostly from the cloud and can run several agents at once, which more easily syncs multiple, even disconnected, on-premises AD forests into one tenant, though it supports a narrower feature set than Connect.
flashcards.detail: Cloud Sync's ability to run lightweight agents inside each forest makes it the simpler choice for a merger or acquisition with disconnected AD forests, while Entra Connect's richer sync engine is usually preferred when an organization needs advanced features such as complex custom attribute-filtering rules.

flashcards.front: Sensitivity label scopes: Files & emails vs. Groups & sites
flashcards.back: A sensitivity label scoped to Files & emails protects individual documents and messages with encryption, watermarks, headers/footers, and permission restrictions. A label scoped to Groups & sites instead applies container-level settings to a Microsoft 365 Group, Team, or SharePoint site itself — controlling its privacy (public/private), external user access, and unmanaged device access.
flashcards.detail: A label meant to lock down an entire Team's privacy and guest access must have its Groups & sites scope enabled — the Files & emails scope alone never touches container-level settings, even if it is the only scope an admin remembers to turn on when publishing the label.

flashcards.front: DLP policy and rule priority (evaluation order)
flashcards.back: Microsoft Purview DLP policies are evaluated in priority order, where a lower priority number is evaluated first, and within a policy its rules are evaluated top-down. When a rule's conditions match and its action includes "stop processing more rules," later lower-priority rules and policies are skipped for that item.
flashcards.detail: When two overlapping DLP policies appear to give conflicting results on the same content, the fix is usually reordering policy priority rather than editing either policy's conditions, since priority — not creation date — decides which policy's action actually applies.

flashcards.front: Risk-based Conditional Access: sign-in risk vs. user risk
flashcards.back: Microsoft Entra ID Protection feeds Conditional Access two distinct risk signals: sign-in risk, a real-time, session-specific signal (like an impossible-travel pattern or an anonymous IP), and user risk, an ongoing aggregate likelihood that the account itself is compromised (such as a leaked-credential match). Policies can require different responses for each, like MFA for elevated sign-in risk versus a secure password change for high user risk.
flashcards.detail: The two risk types remediate differently: satisfying MFA for one risky sign-in clears that session's sign-in risk, but it does not clear high user risk from leaked credentials — that typically requires the user to actually change their password.

flashcards.front: Adaptive scopes in Microsoft Purview
flashcards.back: Adaptive scopes dynamically include users, groups, or sites in a retention policy (and in other Purview solutions, such as DLP for SharePoint sites and Insider Risk Management) based on attribute-based queries (like department = Finance) rather than a fixed, manually maintained list, so the policy's coverage recalculates automatically as attributes or group membership change.
flashcards.detail: Adaptive scopes are only as accurate as the underlying attributes — a stale or incorrect department value in Microsoft Entra ID silently changes who a policy protects, since the scope is recalculated from that attribute rather than from a list an admin explicitly reviews.

flashcards.front: Compliance Manager assessment templates
flashcards.back: Compliance Manager ships regulatory and Microsoft-recommended assessment templates (such as GDPR, ISO 27001, or NIST) that an admin adds to build an assessment; each template translates its requirements into tracked improvement actions with assigned point values, and an organization can run multiple assessments concurrently to track several regulations at once.
flashcards.detail: The same underlying control, like enabling MFA, often counts toward more than one assessment's score at the same time, because overlapping regulatory templates frequently share the same underlying requirement.

flashcards.front: Who can search the Microsoft Purview audit log
flashcards.back: Searching the unified audit log in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal requires a role with audit search rights (such as Audit Reader or Audit Manager, or a broader compliance role like Compliance Administrator), and audit logging must be turned on for the tenant, which it is by default in modern tenants.
flashcards.detail: Audit Reader is the least-privileged option because it includes only the View-Only Audit Logs role, while Audit Manager adds the ability to manage audit log settings and retention policies, so granting the narrower role group fits an analyst who only needs to search.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
flashcards.back: PIM lets admin roles be assigned as eligible rather than permanently active, so a user must explicitly activate the role — often satisfying MFA and providing a business justification — for a limited time window when they actually need it, shrinking the number of standing privileged accounts available to an attacker.
flashcards.detail: PIM can also require a designated approver to sign off before an eligible role activates, and every activation, approval, and expiration is recorded in the audit log, producing a clear record of exactly when and why elevated access was used instead of access simply being always-on.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Copilot usage reporting
flashcards.back: Copilot usage reports in the Microsoft 365 admin center, alongside the Viva Insights Copilot Dashboard, show adoption metrics like active users, which apps Copilot is used in, and usage trends over time, letting admins measure rollout success and spot licensed users who are not adopting Copilot.
flashcards.detail: These reports measure activity (who used Copilot, in which apps, and how often), not content, so an admin cannot use them to see what one specific person asked Copilot — that level of detail requires a targeted eDiscovery search instead.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat vs. licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot
flashcards.back: Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat (now Microsoft Copilot Chat; the evolution of Bing Chat Enterprise) is included at no extra cost with any Microsoft Entra work account and provides web-grounded chat with some limited file-grounded help. The fully licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on goes further, grounding responses in the organization's own Semantic Index across emails, files, and chats, and embedding Copilot directly inside apps like Word, Excel, and Outlook.
flashcards.detail: Because Copilot Chat is available to nearly every user by default, an organization that has purchased zero Copilot add-on licenses can still have employees genuinely "using Copilot" — governance and DLP planning need to account for this free tier too, not only the paid add-on.

flashcards.front: Governing Copilot extensibility: plugins and published agents
flashcards.back: Admins control which third-party plugins, Graph connectors, and published Copilot agents are available tenant-wide through the agent management settings of the Copilot Control System in the Microsoft 365 admin center (the Agents area of the admin center, which replaced Integrated apps), letting them allow, block, or scope specific extensions to designated groups instead of leaving extensibility ungoverned.
flashcards.detail: Publishing a custom agent in Copilot Studio does not by itself make it available tenant-wide — an admin's approval and deployment settings in agent management are often what actually gate whether other users can find and use it, not the act of publishing.

flashcards.front: Copilot Studio message capacity and pay-as-you-go billing
flashcards.back: Copilot Studio agent usage draws first from prepaid capacity (capacity packs bought for the tenant), and once that allotment is exhausted, additional usage is billed on a metered, pay-as-you-go basis if enabled, or the agent may stop responding until the next capacity period if it is not. Copilot Studio meters usage in Copilot Credits (formerly called messages), while internal agents used by people who hold a Microsoft 365 Copilot license are covered by that license.
flashcards.detail: A heavily used custom agent that serves unlicensed users can quietly consume far more than its prepaid capacity — admins should monitor capacity reports rather than assume a fixed fee covers unlimited custom-agent usage.

flashcards.front: EU Data Boundary and Microsoft 365 Copilot data processing
flashcards.back: The EU Data Boundary lets in-scope EU/EFTA customers keep the storage and processing of their Microsoft 365 data — including Copilot prompts, grounding data, and generated responses — within the EU/EFTA region, limiting when that data is transferred outside the boundary.
flashcards.detail: Enabling the EU Data Boundary is a tenant-wide data-residency commitment, not a Copilot-only toggle, and coverage of specific Copilot experiences has expanded over time — an admin should confirm which particular features are actually in scope rather than assuming everything was covered from day one.

flashcards.front: Break-glass (emergency access) accounts
flashcards.back: Break-glass accounts are highly privileged, cloud-only accounts deliberately kept outside normal identity lifecycle rules and excluded from Conditional Access policies that could block them, so an admin can still sign in if Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) approval workflows, Conditional Access policies, or an MFA provider all become unavailable at once. Current Microsoft guidance is to protect them with a phishing-resistant method such as a FIDO2 security key rather than leaving them without MFA.
flashcards.detail: Because they sit outside the normal Conditional Access safety net and are closely monitored for any sign-in activity, a break-glass account being used at all should trigger an investigation, not just be treated as a routine login.

flashcards.front: Access reviews
flashcards.back: Access reviews let an admin schedule periodic, recurring recertification of who still needs a given assignment — a role activated through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM), a security group membership, or a guest's access to a resource — requiring a reviewer to explicitly approve or deny continued access instead of it persisting indefinitely by default.
flashcards.detail: Unlike a GDAP relationship, whose time-bound scoping is built into the access itself, an access review's recurrence has to be actively scheduled, and what happens when reviewers do not respond depends on the configured default decision (no change, remove access, approve access, or take the system recommendation) — leaving it at no change quietly undoes the point of the recertification.

flashcards.front: Email authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC
flashcards.back: SPF publishes a DNS TXT record listing which mail servers are authorized to send on behalf of a domain. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to each outgoing message, verified against a public key published in DNS. DMARC tells receiving servers what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail — monitor, quarantine, or reject — and where to send aggregate failure reports.
flashcards.detail: DMARC is the layer that actually sets a disposition and generates reporting; SPF and DKIM only establish whether a message passes authentication, neither one alone says what a receiving server should then do about a failure.

flashcards.front: Usage location on a user account
flashcards.back: Usage location is a required attribute on a user's profile that determines which licenses and services can legally be assigned to them, since some countries and regions have service availability restrictions. A license cannot be assigned to a profile with no usage location set.
flashcards.detail: Group-based licensing doesn't bypass this requirement — a group member with no usage location set is skipped and flagged as a licensing error instead of silently receiving the license.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra dynamic groups (membership rule-based)
flashcards.back: A dynamic group (security or Microsoft 365 group) automatically adds or removes members based on a membership rule evaluated against attributes like department or job title, instead of someone manually curating the member list by hand.
flashcards.detail: This is what lets group-based licensing scale with no manual membership upkeep, since the group's own membership stays current on its own as attributes change.

flashcards.front: Global Reader vs. Reports Reader admin roles
flashcards.back: Global Reader grants read-only visibility into nearly every admin center and configuration setting a Global Administrator could view, with no edit rights at all, which suits an auditor. Reports Reader grants a much narrower read-only view, limited specifically to usage reports and reporting dashboards.
flashcards.detail: This is least-privilege delegation applied to oversight: Global Reader exists specifically so an auditor never needs standing edit rights just to review configuration end to end.

flashcards.front: Multi-Geo capabilities in Microsoft 365
flashcards.back: Multi-Geo lets a single tenant store a given user's primary mailbox, OneDrive, and SharePoint data in a geographic region of choice (a satellite location), while the organization remains one tenant with one directory, instead of operating a fully separate tenant per region.
flashcards.detail: This differs from the EU Data Boundary, which governs whether an entire in-scope tenant's data (including Copilot data processing) stays within the EU/EFTA region — Multi-Geo instead controls where a given user's own data physically sits within one tenant spanning several regions.

flashcards.front: Teams meeting and messaging policies
flashcards.back: Meeting policies control what participants can do in Teams meetings — recording, transcription, who can present. Messaging policies control chat capabilities — editing or deleting sent messages, stickers and Giphy. Both are assigned per user or group, and policy packages bundle several related policies together for a role like Frontline Worker.
flashcards.detail: This is a workload-configuration control, not an identity-layer one — a user needing different meeting behavior gets a different Teams policy assigned, not a change to a Conditional Access policy.

flashcards.front: Entra ID Governance entitlement management (access packages)
flashcards.back: Entitlement management lets admins bundle resources — group membership, a Team, a SharePoint site, an app — into an access package that users can request through a self-service catalog, with built-in approval workflows and automatic expiration, instead of an admin manually granting each resource one at a time.
flashcards.detail: An access package's automatic expiration already builds in the recertification that an access review would otherwise have to be scheduled separately to provide for a group or role assignment created outside entitlement management.

flashcards.front: Admin consent workflow and app consent policies
flashcards.back: App consent policies control whether a user can consent on their own to let a third-party or custom app access organizational data through Microsoft Graph permissions, or whether such requests must instead be routed to an admin through the admin consent workflow for explicit approval.
flashcards.detail: This governs the same kind of permission-granting exposure that an ungoverned Copilot agent or plugin could otherwise exploit — requiring admin consent closes the gap where a user could unknowingly approve broad Graph access just to install a convenient add-in.

flashcards.front: Privileged Access Groups (PIM for Groups)
flashcards.back: Privileged Access Groups extend the just-in-time, time-bound activation model of Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) to security groups and Microsoft 365 groups themselves, so a group's own owner or member role can be made eligible rather than standing, not only individual Microsoft Entra admin roles.
flashcards.detail: Applying PIM to a group is what lets a group that in turn grants a Microsoft Entra role, an app role, or a license assignment be governed with eligible, time-bound membership instead of standing membership.

flashcards.front: Preservation Lock on a retention policy
flashcards.back: Preservation Lock on a Microsoft Purview retention policy prevents anyone, including a Global Administrator, from turning the policy off or shortening its retention period once locked, until the locked duration itself expires, guaranteeing a regulatory retention commitment can't quietly be weakened later.
flashcards.detail: Without Preservation Lock, an ordinary retention policy can still be edited or disabled by an administrator at any time — this feature exists specifically to close that gap for regulatory retention commitments.

flashcards.front: Authentication strength (phishing-resistant MFA requirement)
flashcards.back: Authentication strength is a Conditional Access grant control that requires sign-in with a specific combination of authentication methods, such as mandating a phishing-resistant method (FIDO2 key, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based authentication) rather than accepting any MFA method equally.
flashcards.detail: It is a more granular grant control than a plain 'require MFA' rule, since it can demand a specific method instead of accepting any second factor, including a weaker one like SMS.

flashcards.front: Declarative agents vs. custom engine agents in Copilot Studio
flashcards.back: A declarative agent is built on top of Microsoft 365 Copilot's own orchestrator and Semantic Index, configured mainly through instructions, knowledge sources, and actions with little code. A custom engine agent instead brings its own independent reasoning engine and language model, giving full control at the cost of far more development effort.
flashcards.detail: An agent created from a SharePoint site is a simple example of a declarative agent, while a fully bespoke agent built with its own model and orchestration logic is a custom engine agent.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 admin center Copilot settings page
flashcards.back: The Copilot page in the Microsoft 365 admin center is the starting point for tenant-wide Copilot settings, such as enabling or disabling web search (letting Copilot search the public web for extra context; the underlying Allow web search in Copilot policy is configured through the Cloud Policy service), and managing which connectors and agents are available.
flashcards.detail: This settings page is one of the concrete admin surfaces that makes up the broader Copilot Control System governance umbrella, alongside Purview's data and compliance controls.

flashcards.front: Cross-prompt injection and content safety protections for Copilot
flashcards.back: Cross-prompt injection is when malicious instructions hidden in a document, email, or web page that Copilot reads as grounding content attempt to hijack its response or trick it into taking an unintended action. Microsoft 365 Copilot includes built-in content safety classifiers and prompt-shielding protections specifically designed to detect and block this kind of hidden-instruction attack.
flashcards.detail: This risk is distinct from oversharing, because Copilot grants no new access: oversharing is about Copilot surfacing content a user can already see, while cross-prompt injection is about an attacker using grounding content as a vector to manipulate Copilot's behavior itself.

flashcards.front: Copilot Studio generative orchestration vs. classic orchestration
flashcards.back: Classic (topic-based) orchestration follows a fixed set of author-defined conversation topics and trigger phrases to decide how to respond. Generative orchestration instead lets the agent's underlying model dynamically decide, at runtime, which topics, knowledge sources, or actions best answer a given message, reducing how much of every conversation path has to be manually authored.
flashcards.detail: An agent author can mix both: a few tightly controlled classic topics for sensitive actions, with generative orchestration filling in open-ended questions the fixed topics don't cover.

flashcards.front: Power Platform data loss prevention (DLP) policies and Copilot Studio connectors
flashcards.back: Power Platform DLP policies classify connectors into groups — such as Business, Non-Business, and Blocked — and determine which connectors a Copilot Studio agent, Power Automate flow, or Power App running in a given environment is allowed to combine in the same action. This is a separate governance layer from Purview DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot interactions and governs what an agent can call, not what sensitive content it can surface.
flashcards.detail: DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot stops sensitive content from appearing in a Copilot response; a Power Platform DLP policy instead stops a Copilot Studio agent from ever being built to combine an approved connector with a blocked one in the first place.

flashcards.front: SharePoint Advanced Management: restricted access control
flashcards.back: Restricted access control, part of SharePoint Advanced Management, lets an admin limit access to a given SharePoint site to members of a specified security group or Microsoft 365 group, even for users who otherwise hold broader permissions on the site — a true access restriction, not just a search-visibility change.
flashcards.detail: This goes further than Restricted SharePoint Search, which only affects what appears in search and Copilot results while leaving every existing permission intact; restricted access control can actually cut off access to the site itself.

flashcards.front: SharePoint Advanced Management: data access governance reports
flashcards.back: Data access governance reports, part of SharePoint Advanced Management, surface where SharePoint and OneDrive content is exposed — for example sites with many new sharing links, content shared with "Everyone except external users," and the distribution of sensitivity labels — giving admins a prioritized list of sites to remediate before or during a wider Microsoft 365 Copilot rollout.
flashcards.detail: These reports identify where oversharing risk concentrates at the site level, complementing DSPM for AI, which instead reports on what AI tools actually did with that content once a user prompted against it.

flashcards.front: Copilot Pages
flashcards.back: A Copilot Page is a persistent, shareable canvas that Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat can generate from a conversation, letting a user move an AI-generated draft out of a one-off chat response into a document multiple people can keep open, edit, and co-author together.
flashcards.detail: Because a Page is a durable artifact rather than a disappearing chat reply, the same governance surfaces that apply to other Copilot output — such as auditing and eDiscovery — extend to what gets written into a Page as well.

flashcards.front: Built-in named Copilot agents (Facilitator, Interpreter, Researcher, Analyst, Project Manager)
flashcards.back: Microsoft ships several purpose-built, first-party Copilot agents inside Microsoft 365 apps rather than requiring every org to build its own — for example, Facilitator summarizes and tracks action items live inside a Teams meeting, Interpreter provides real-time speech translation, and Researcher, Analyst, and Project Manager bring deeper reasoning or task-tracking into Microsoft 365 Copilot and Planner.
flashcards.detail: These differ from a custom agent built in Copilot Studio — they ship ready-made from Microsoft and are governed through the same Copilot Control System settings rather than through an org's own agent-build process.

flashcards.front: Copilot Studio agent publishing channels
flashcards.back: A Copilot Studio agent can be published to more than one surface at once — inside Microsoft Teams, embedded in Microsoft 365 Copilot, exposed as a custom website chat widget, or reached through a direct line / API channel — and each channel can be enabled or disabled independently for the same underlying agent.
flashcards.detail: Disabling a channel stops that particular surface from reaching the agent without deleting or republishing it, which is a faster way to pull a misbehaving agent off one surface (say, a public website) while leaving its internal Teams availability untouched.

flashcards.front: Scoping Conditional Access to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio sign-in
flashcards.back: Because Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio authenticate through Microsoft Entra, a Conditional Access policy can target them as cloud apps in their own right (for Microsoft 365 Copilot, the Enterprise Copilot Platform service principal, which may first need to be created so it appears in the app picker) — for example, blocking Copilot access from a disallowed country or requiring a compliant device specifically before Copilot sign-in succeeds, without changing sign-in requirements for the rest of Microsoft 365.
flashcards.detail: This lets an admin apply a narrower rule to Copilot specifically than to Microsoft 365 generally, layering on top of — rather than replacing — the broader Conditional Access policies already governing sign-in.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Copilot readiness assessment vs. usage reporting
flashcards.back: A Copilot readiness assessment runs before a rollout, scoring factors like identity hygiene, device compliance, and data governance (oversharing risk) to flag what should be fixed first. Microsoft 365 Copilot usage reporting instead runs after rollout, measuring adoption and active-usage trends once licenses are already assigned.
flashcards.detail: Treating usage reporting as a stand-in for readiness is a common mistake — a high adoption number after rollout says nothing about whether oversharing or stale permissions were ever actually cleaned up beforehand.

flashcards.front: Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)
flashcards.back: Continuous Access Evaluation lets Microsoft Entra ID and supporting services revoke or re-evaluate an access token near real time when a critical event happens — a user is disabled, a password is changed, or a Conditional Access location condition is violated — instead of waiting for the token's normal lifetime to expire.
flashcards.detail: Without CAE, a revoked user's existing access token could otherwise keep working until its scheduled expiry; CAE is what closes that window down to roughly minutes instead of up to the token's full remaining lifetime.

flashcards.front: Records Management: regulatory records vs. standard retention labels
flashcards.back: A standard retention label still lets an authorized user remove the label or, in some configurations, edit the underlying content. Declaring an item a regulatory record through Microsoft Purview Records Management locks it down so that even its label and key properties can't be changed or removed by anyone, including an admin, until its retention period genuinely runs out.
flashcards.detail: This is the item-level counterpart of Preservation Lock, which protects a whole retention policy — once an item is declared a regulatory record, the restriction stays in force until the retention period ends, and an administrator cannot simply remove it.

flashcards.front: Exact Data Match (EDM) sensitive information types
flashcards.back: A standard sensitive information type matches a pattern, like a string of digits shaped like a credit card number, so it can flag something that merely looks sensitive. An Exact Data Match (EDM) sensitive information type instead checks content against an actual, uploaded dataset of real values — like a company's genuine employee ID list — catching only true matches and sharply cutting down false positives.
flashcards.detail: EDM is the right answer whenever a scenario specifically says a DLP or auto-labeling policy keeps flagging content that merely resembles sensitive data, rather than real, current records.

flashcards.front: Mandatory (default) sensitivity labeling policies
flashcards.back: A mandatory labeling policy requires a user to apply some sensitivity label before they can save a document or send an email, rather than only recommending a label or relying on auto-labeling to catch it afterward. It is commonly paired with a separate default label setting, so the user starts with a label already selected and cannot remove it entirely.
flashcards.detail: This closes a gap that auto-labeling alone leaves open: auto-labeling can take time to apply retroactively, while a mandatory policy stops an unlabeled item from ever being saved or sent in the first place.

flashcards.front: Self-service password reset (SSPR) registration vs. reset method counts
flashcards.back: SSPR lets an admin set how many authentication methods a user must provide to reset a password (one or two), and users must register at least that many methods. Encouraging users to register more methods than a reset requires — for example, three registered methods with one needed at reset — means a user who loses access to one method can still recover their account.
flashcards.detail: Having only the bare minimum of methods registered creates a single point of failure: lose that one method and self-service reset becomes impossible, forcing a helpdesk-assisted reset instead.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Groups naming policy and blocked words
flashcards.back: A groups naming policy can enforce a prefix or suffix convention (like dept- or -grp) on every new Microsoft 365 group and Team, and separately maintain a blocked words list that rejects group names containing specific terms (like executive titles or offensive language) at creation time.
flashcards.detail: This keeps self-service group creation from producing confusingly named or impersonation-prone groups and Teams at scale, without requiring an admin to manually review every group name as it's created.

flashcards.front: Teams external access (federation) vs. guest access
flashcards.back: External access (federation) lets users in one organization's tenant chat, call, and meet with users in another organization's tenant without either side becoming a member of the other's tenant. Guest access instead adds an external user as an actual Microsoft Entra B2B guest member of a specific team, giving them persistent access to that team's channels, files, and apps.
flashcards.detail: A vendor who should be able to message your employees occasionally needs external access; a long-term contractor who needs to sit inside one specific Team's channels and files day after day needs to be added as a guest instead.

flashcards.front: Cloud Policy service for Microsoft 365
flashcards.back: A service in the Microsoft 365 Apps admin center that enforces Office policy settings, much like Group Policy, on Microsoft 365 Apps wherever a targeted user signs in, even on devices that are not domain joined or otherwise managed.
flashcards.detail: Policies apply to users and Microsoft Entra groups, not devices. The Allow web search in Copilot policy is one of the settings an admin can configure here.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra administrative units
flashcards.back: Containers that subdivide a tenant so a role assignment can be limited to the users, groups, or devices inside that unit instead of applying tenant-wide. They let you delegate administration without granting broad rights.
flashcards.detail: A Helpdesk Administrator scoped to the Sales administrative unit can reset passwords only for Sales users and cannot change tenant-wide settings.

flashcards.front: Global Administrator role
flashcards.back: The most privileged Microsoft Entra role, with access to nearly every administrative feature and the ability to assign any other role. Microsoft recommends fewer than five Global Administrators and using narrower roles for daily work.
flashcards.detail: Exam angle: when a scenario needs only one task, such as resetting passwords or reading reports, the answer is a least-privilege role, not Global Administrator.

flashcards.front: User Administrator vs. Helpdesk Administrator
flashcards.back: User Administrator can create and manage users and groups, assign licenses, and reset passwords for users and some limited admin roles. Helpdesk Administrator can reset passwords and sign users out, but only for non-administrators and other helpdesk admins, and cannot create users.
flashcards.detail: A support tier that only unlocks accounts needs Helpdesk Administrator. Onboarding staff who must create accounts and assign licenses needs User Administrator.

flashcards.front: Service principal vs. app registration
flashcards.back: An app registration is the definition of an application in Microsoft Entra ID. A service principal is that app's identity inside a specific tenant, appearing as an enterprise application, where permissions and access are actually granted.
flashcards.detail: Admins assign permissions and Conditional Access to the service principal. That is why the Copilot sign-in policy targets a service principal rather than an app registration.

flashcards.front: Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)
flashcards.back: An on-premises service that provides federated sign-in. With federation, Microsoft Entra ID redirects authentication to AD FS, so passwords are validated by your own infrastructure instead of in the cloud.
flashcards.detail: It gives the most control but needs servers you must keep highly available. Password hash sync is the simplest hybrid choice, which is why moving off AD FS is a common simplification.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra ID P1 vs. P2
flashcards.back: P1 adds premium features such as Conditional Access, dynamic groups, and self-service password reset with writeback. P2 includes everything in P1 and adds Microsoft Entra ID Protection with risk-based Conditional Access, plus Privileged Identity Management.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario needs sign-in risk or user risk policies, or just-in-time admin elevation, the license answer is P2. Basic Conditional Access alone only needs P1.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra ID Protection
flashcards.back: A service that detects identity risks, such as risky sign-ins and risky users, using signals like leaked credentials, impossible travel, and anonymous IP addresses. It feeds those risk levels into Conditional Access for automatic responses. It needs Microsoft Entra ID P2.
flashcards.detail: A user flagged with high user risk can be forced to change their password, while a risky sign-in can require MFA. The signal drives the policy, not the other way around.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
flashcards.back: A cloud access security broker that discovers which cloud apps people use, controls access and sessions to them, and detects unusual activity. Session controls work through Conditional Access to limit what users can do inside an app.
flashcards.detail: Blocking downloads of labeled files from an unmanaged device, while still allowing browser viewing, is a classic session-policy use case.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 plans (Plan 1 and Plan 2)
flashcards.back: Plan 1 gives preventive protection: Safe Links, Safe Attachments, and anti-phishing with impersonation detection. Plan 2 adds investigation and response, including Threat Explorer, automated investigation and response (AIR), campaigns, and Attack simulation training.
flashcards.detail: A scenario that asks to hunt for a phishing message across mailboxes, or to remediate it automatically, needs Plan 2. Blocking bad links at click time is already Plan 1.

flashcards.front: Legacy authentication
flashcards.back: Older sign-in methods, such as IMAP, POP, SMTP AUTH, and some older Office clients using basic authentication, that cannot perform multifactor authentication. Attackers use them for password spray because MFA cannot stop them.
flashcards.detail: Security defaults block legacy authentication automatically. With Conditional Access, you create a policy that blocks it yourself.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Authenticator number matching
flashcards.back: When approving a sign-in in the Microsoft Authenticator app, the user must type a number shown on the sign-in screen into the app. This makes it much harder to approve a request by accident or under pressure.
flashcards.detail: It counters MFA fatigue, where an attacker floods a user with push prompts hoping for one tap. A plain approve button gives no proof the user started the sign-in.

flashcards.front: Temporary Access Pass (TAP)
flashcards.back: A time-limited passcode issued by an admin that lets a user sign in without a password to register passwordless methods, such as a FIDO2 key or Authenticator, or to recover access. It can be set as one-time use or multi-use.
flashcards.detail: Use it for a new hire's first sign-in or a user who lost their phone. It bootstraps passwordless credentials without ever giving a permanent password.

flashcards.front: Conditional Access report-only mode
flashcards.back: A policy state that evaluates a Conditional Access policy for each sign-in and logs what would have happened, without enforcing it. Admins review the results before turning the policy on.
flashcards.detail: Putting a new block-by-location policy in report-only first reveals which legitimate users it would lock out. It is the safe way to test before enforcement.

flashcards.front: Named locations in Conditional Access
flashcards.back: Defined sets of IP address ranges, or countries and regions, that a Conditional Access policy can use as a condition. A named location can be marked trusted, such as an office network.
flashcards.detail: Require MFA for every sign-in except from the trusted office range, or block sign-ins from countries where the company has no staff. Both use named locations.

flashcards.front: Sensitive information types (SITs)
flashcards.back: Pattern-based detectors for data like credit card or national ID numbers, using regular expressions, keywords, checksums, and a confidence level. Microsoft Purview uses them in DLP, auto-labeling, and retention.
flashcards.detail: Use a SIT when data has a recognizable format. For documents defined by their content rather than a pattern, a trainable classifier is the better tool.

flashcards.front: Trainable classifiers
flashcards.back: Machine learning models that recognize a category of content, such as contracts or source code, by learning from sample documents instead of matching a pattern. Microsoft provides built-in ones, and you can train your own.
flashcards.detail: A SIT finds a credit card number. A trainable classifier recognizes a whole document as, say, a financial statement and can then drive a label or retention policy.

flashcards.front: Endpoint data loss prevention (Endpoint DLP)
flashcards.back: Extends Microsoft Purview DLP to files on onboarded Windows and macOS devices, so admins can audit or restrict actions such as copying to USB, uploading to cloud services, printing, or copying to the clipboard.
flashcards.detail: Preventing a labeled file from going to a USB drive needs Endpoint DLP. Exchange and SharePoint DLP locations cannot see what happens on a local device.

flashcards.front: DLP policy tips and user overrides
flashcards.back: A policy tip is a notice in the app telling a user that content conflicts with a DLP policy. An override lets the user proceed after giving a business justification or reporting a false positive, and the action is still logged.
flashcards.detail: A rule in simulation mode with tips off collects data silently. Allowing overrides keeps work moving but still records who bypassed the rule and why.

flashcards.front: Preservation Hold library
flashcards.back: A hidden library in a SharePoint site or OneDrive where Microsoft Purview keeps a copy of the original of any item changed or deleted while subject to retention. The copy stays until the retention period ends.
flashcards.detail: A user deletes a contract that is under a retention policy: it vanishes from the site but remains in the Preservation Hold library. It is for retention and eDiscovery, not user recovery.

flashcards.front: Recoverable Items folder
flashcards.back: A hidden Exchange mailbox folder that holds deleted items and retained copies for holds and retention. Teams and Copilot interaction data under retention is kept in its SubstrateHolds subfolder.
flashcards.detail: A litigation hold on a mailbox keeps items here even after the user empties Deleted Items. It is the Exchange counterpart of the Preservation Hold library.

flashcards.front: Adaptive Protection
flashcards.back: A Microsoft Purview feature linking Insider Risk Management with DLP. It assigns users an insider risk level of elevated, moderate, or minor and applies stricter DLP controls to higher-risk users, relaxing them as risk drops.
flashcards.detail: Instead of blocking everyone, a policy can apply tough restrictions only to users whose behavior has raised their risk level, so low-risk users keep working normally.

flashcards.front: Enterprise data protection (EDP) for Copilot Chat
flashcards.back: When a user signs in with a Microsoft Entra work account, Copilot Chat prompts and responses are protected: encrypted, isolated per tenant, and not used to train foundation models. It also honors permissions, sensitivity labels, retention, and auditing.
flashcards.detail: It is why Copilot Chat is acceptable for work content even for users with no Copilot license, unlike a consumer chat tool with a personal account.

flashcards.front: Restricted Content Discovery (RCD)
flashcards.back: A SharePoint Advanced Management setting that keeps content from selected SharePoint sites out of organization-wide search and Microsoft 365 Copilot, without changing any site permissions. It replaces Restricted SharePoint Search.
flashcards.detail: It is a visibility control, not a security boundary: users who already have access can still open the files, and it applies to SharePoint sites, not OneDrive. It also removes AI entry points such as the Copilot button on those sites. Use restricted access control to truly limit who can access a site.

flashcards.front: SharePoint Advanced Management: site access review
flashcards.back: A feature that lets an admin start a review in which site owners confirm whether the content shared on their site is appropriate, then fix excess permissions through a dashboard.
flashcards.detail: After data access governance reports flag an overshared site, a site access review puts the cleanup in the hands of the people who know the content best.

flashcards.front: Copilot Dashboard in Viva Insights
flashcards.back: A dashboard in Viva Insights (part of Copilot Analytics) showing readiness, adoption, and impact metrics for Microsoft 365 Copilot, aimed at helping leaders see how Copilot is changing work, beyond simply counting active users.
flashcards.detail: Admin center usage reports show who is using Copilot. The Copilot Dashboard is where leaders look to judge whether adoption is producing business impact.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Copilot Notebooks
flashcards.back: A workspace in Microsoft 365 Copilot where a user gathers chats, files, pages, meeting notes, and links for a topic, then asks Copilot to find answers and themes across that material. Notebooks can be shared with teammates.
flashcards.detail: A project lead can collect all project materials in one notebook and ask for a status summary. It needs a Microsoft 365 Copilot or Copilot Chat license.

flashcards.front: Copilot Studio knowledge sources
flashcards.back: The content a Copilot Studio agent uses to answer generatively, such as SharePoint sites, Dataverse, public websites, uploaded files, and Copilot connectors. For enterprise sources, the agent's answers follow the user's own permissions.
flashcards.detail: An agent given a wiki as a knowledge source answers questions from it, but that does not make the wiki available to Microsoft 365 Copilot in general.

flashcards.front: Web search (web grounding) in Microsoft 365 Copilot
flashcards.back: When enabled, Copilot can create a short search query, sent to Bing, to add public web information to an answer. The query is not the full prompt and does not include the user's Microsoft Entra identity details.
flashcards.detail: Admins control it with the Allow web search in Copilot policy. Turning it off does not stop Copilot from grounding in work data, and a DLP policy does not toggle it.

flashcards.front: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
flashcards.back: An open standard for exposing tools and knowledge to AI agents. When an MCP server is added to a Copilot Studio agent, each tool the server exposes becomes available for the agent to call during a conversation.
flashcards.detail: It lets makers connect an agent to existing systems quickly. For admins, each MCP server an agent can reach is another extension to review, like a connector or plugin.

flashcards.front: Sensitivity label inheritance in Copilot
flashcards.back: Copilot responses, and new files it creates from labeled content, take the highest-priority sensitivity label among the sources used. Label priority is set in Microsoft Purview, with higher priority meaning more restrictive.
flashcards.detail: Summarizing a General file and a Confidential file gives a Confidential result. The label follows the most sensitive source, so protection is not lost in the new content.

flashcards.front: Usage rights VIEW and EXTRACT for Copilot
flashcards.back: For encrypted content, Copilot returns it to a user only if that user has both the VIEW and EXTRACT usage rights. Content protected without the EXTRACT right stays hidden from Copilot even if the user can open it.
flashcards.detail: Do Not Forward leaves out EXTRACT, so a user may see an email yet get nothing from Copilot about it. Check the label's usage rights when Copilot cannot find protected content.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Agent 365
flashcards.back: A control plane for governing AI agents across the organization (generally available for commercial customers since May 1, 2026, licensed per user and included in Microsoft 365 E7).
